name: Felix Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying computer engineering in Turin, and I share a flat with my cousin Matteo, who does architecture. A normal week is lectures from eight, labs on Tuesdays and Fridays, and the rest is me hacking on a project, an ordering app for restaurants. It's not an accident, because my family owns a pizzeria and two small restaurants in Asti, and every Sunday I go home and help in the kitchen. I use AI tools every day, I'd say for half of what I do. My parents pay for everything, and my nonna still slips me 50 euros when she thinks nobody sees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the restaurants still need pizza and the world still needs coders. I'd tell my cousin Matteo he owes me a coffee, because he bet it would change everything. Online I'd post a photo of a pizza.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a little let down, but my family's businesses would carry on as before. Pizza ovens aren't going away. I'd still keep an eye on food prices and rents, since those squeeze my parents more than AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my ordering app and put it in my parents' pizzeria for real, with real customers. I'd apply for a summer job at a software company in Turin, and I'd keep using AI tools because they make me faster even if they're not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A normal world, a normal job at the end, and a pizza at home on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said food prices squeeze your parents. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said food prices squeeze your parents. How? Flour, cheese and energy have all gone up, and customers won't pay much more. My father says some months the margin in his pizzeria is the price of a coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your app do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does your app do about it? It cuts waste by predicting orders, so they buy less and throw away less. It's small, but it could save a few hundred euros a month.

say: I'd say good, restaurants still need **pizza** and the world still needs coders.
I'd tell Matteo (his cousin) he owes me a **coffee**.
think: I'd be a little let down, but the **family businesses** carry on as before.
Food prices and **rents** squeeze my parents more than AI does.
do: Put my **ordering app** into my parents' pizzeria with real customers.
Apply for a summer job at a **software company** in Turin.
Keep using **AI tools** because they make me faster.
feel: **Calm**: a normal world, a normal job, and pizza on Sundays.
S0.quote: My father says some months the margin in his pizzeria is the price of a coffee.
fieldNote: Felix is **calm**, because his parents' trade is physical and he's already building.
The real squeeze is food prices and rents, not AI.
His app aims at waste, a practical use that earns money.

steps.text: Put the ordering app into my parents' pizzeria for real
Apply for a summer job at a Turin software company
Keep using AI tools for coding and lab work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big chance if you move early. I'd tell my family: let's use the tools for ordering, menus and bookings, so we're ahead of the other restaurants in Asti. Online I'd post how I did it, because I like showing off a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd see two sides. Restaurants have hands-on work, so they're safe for a while, but the big delivery platforms will use AI to squeeze the small ones. And my own junior coding jobs would be fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd roll out my app to three restaurants in Asti, not just ours, and charge a small fee. I'd learn to build with AI agents so the app can answer booking calls. And I'd put what I earn into new kitchen equipment for my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit electric. I feel I'm in a race, and I like races, but I can see my family isn't built for racing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why isn't your family built for racing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why isn't your family built for racing? My father wakes at five, bakes, serves and closes at midnight, so he has no time to learn tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to him? That I'll build it and he can stay the pizza maker. He'd say he's proud, then complain I'm working too much.

say: I'd say it's a **big chance** if you move early.
I'd tell my family to use tools for **ordering, menus and bookings**.
think: Delivery platforms will use AI to **squeeze** small restaurants.
My own junior coding jobs would be **fewer**, so I need my own projects.
do: Roll out the app to **three restaurants** in Asti and charge a small fee.
Learn to build with **AI agents** that answer booking calls.
Put what I earn into new **kitchen equipment**.
feel: **Uneasy** and electric; I like races, but my family isn't built for one.
S1.quote: My father wakes at five, bakes, serves and closes at midnight, so he has no time to learn tools.
fieldNote: Felix wants to **carry the technology** for his father.
He sees delivery platforms as the real threat.
He's competitive and open about liking to show off.

steps.text: Roll out the ordering app to three restaurants in Asti
Build a booking-call agent for the pizzeria
Buy a second oven for my parents with the app's earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should stay calm and look after our own first: family, church, neighbours. I'd say it's the free market that will find new jobs, but only if the government doesn't get in the way. Honestly, I'd say it more loudly than I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared. My customers, the people who eat in my parents' restaurants, would lose income, and a restaurant needs people with spare cash. The kitchen work is safe until 2031, but nobody would be there to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my parents and work out how long the businesses can survive on a quarter less income. I'd put my effort into the app and into a second business of my own. I'd also ask my nonna, who has savings, to keep them safe and not lend them out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep well, and I'd call my father every day. In the end I'd feel I'm the only one who can do something, which is heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the free market still the answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is the free market still the answer? I'd say yes in the long run, but in the short run it's not enough. I'd want families and the local community to hold things together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the restaurants closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if the restaurants closed? Rent out the premises, go back to the kitchen myself, and keep building. It'd hurt my pride and my nonna's heart, but I'd do it.

say: I'd say stay calm and look after our **own first**: family, church, neighbours.
I'd say the **free market** will find new jobs, though I'd say it louder than I believe it.
think: Customers who eat in my parents' restaurants would **lose income**.
The kitchen work is safe till 2031, but **nobody would pay**.
do: Work out how long the businesses survive on a **quarter less** income.
Put my effort into the app and a **second business**.
Ask Nonna to keep her **savings safe**.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd call my father every day and feel the weight.
S2.quote: The kitchen work is safe until 2031, but nobody would be there to pay.
fieldNote: His alarm is about **customers losing income**, not about the kitchen work.
He says free markets are right in the long run but not enough in the short run.
Pride and family are heavy in his answer.

steps.text: Work out with my parents how long the restaurants last on a quarter less income
Launch a second business selling the app to caterers
Ask Nonna to keep her savings safe
Cut the restaurants' menu to dishes with cheap ingredients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if we're smart. I'd tell my friends to build real things and to help their families. And I'd say we should have a plan for small businesses, because they hold towns together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel I have a chance, and I know I'd have to work hard. I'd graduate in 2029, with the app running in a few restaurants and maybe a small company. My parents' businesses would have time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree while growing the app, aiming for ten restaurants by graduation. I'd save a good share of the earnings in a separate account, for my parents' businesses and for me. And I'd keep my Sundays in the kitchen, because that's where I learn what customers want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but driven. I'd like to say I'm calm, but five years with a date makes my chest tight on some mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the app didn't take off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if the app didn't take off? Take a job at a software firm and keep it as a side project. I'm not stubborn about the idea, I'm stubborn about not sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help small restaurants in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would help small restaurants in that world? Cheap tools, simple rules and local banks that lend to them. And customers who still want a person to bring the pizza.

say: I'd say five years is enough if we're **smart**.
I'd say we need a plan for **small businesses**, because they hold towns together.
think: I'd have a **chance**, and I'd have to work hard.
My parents' businesses would have **time to adjust**.
do: Grow the app to **ten restaurants** by graduation.
Save a good share of earnings in a **separate account**.
Keep my **Sundays** in the kitchen to learn what customers want.
feel: **Anxious** but driven; a date makes my chest tight some mornings.
S3.quote: I'm not stubborn about the idea, I'm stubborn about not sitting still.
fieldNote: Five years suits his **builder** mindset, but the date weighs on him.
He wants cheap tools and local banks for small restaurants.
Sundays in the kitchen are his market research.

steps.text: Grow the ordering app to ten restaurants before graduating
Put half of the app's earnings in a separate account
Keep working Sundays in the family kitchen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long, and the danger is people getting lazy. I'd say we should build real things and keep faith with our families. And I'd say it with a smile, because nobody listens to a grumpy twenty-year-old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good. I'd have a decade of work, a company if I'm lucky, and my parents would be near the end of their working lives. I might even take over the pizzeria, with a lot more technology in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at a software firm for two years, and then grow my own company. I'd keep learning every new tool, and I'd invest steadily in a small portfolio. And I'd keep every Sunday in the family kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. Ten years is a runway, and I know how to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you uneasy? If my parents sold up and I had no family trade to fall back on. A tool can be replaced, but a family can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope the pizzeria looks like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you hope the pizzeria looks like in 2036? The same ovens, the same smell, and a very quiet system in the back doing the orders and the books.

say: I'd say ten years is long, and the danger is **getting lazy**.
I'd say build **real things** and keep faith with our families.
think: I'd have a **decade of work** and maybe a company.
I might take over the **pizzeria**, with much more technology in it.
do: Work at a **software firm** for two years, then grow my own company.
Keep learning every new **tool** and invest steadily.
feel: **Calm** and excited; ten years is a runway.
S4.quote: A tool can be replaced, but a family can't.
fieldNote: With a decade, Felix sees a **future pizzeria** with quiet technology.
He's adaptive in method and traditional in what he protects.

steps.text: Work two years at a software firm, then start my own company
Invest a fixed amount monthly in a small portfolio
Keep Sundays in the family kitchen

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my family's businesses depend on customers with jobs, and I'd be mid-degree. The longer ones let me build and prepare. What would help is cheap tools for small businesses, local banks that lend, and a plan so towns don't empty out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that being a tech person and being traditional isn't a contradiction. I use the newest tools to protect the oldest things, like my family's pizzeria.

headlineQuote: I use the newest tools to protect the oldest things, like my family's pizzeria.
portrait: Felix is an 18-year-old **computer engineering** student in Turin who uses AI tools every day and builds an ordering app for restaurants.
His family's pizzeria and two restaurants in Asti pay for his studies, so his **cushion is strong**.
He is traditional and adaptive: he uses the newest tools to protect **family** and local business.
He turns **alarmed** in 2028, because his family's customers would lose income, and calm with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because the restaurants need customers with spare cash.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **cheap tools** for small businesses, local banks that lend and plans for towns.
